title: This is hard
hookLine: Kristin Neff's practice: hand on heart, "this is hard, others feel this too"
last: SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.

lines: WHAT IF THE ONE HURTING IS YOU?
ONE HAND, A FEW PLAIN WORDS.
cards: A friend in pain gets patience and a gentle voice. The inner voice, on a bad day, can sound more like a drill sergeant. So what about when the one who's hurting is you?
The psychologist Kristin Neff, who studies self-compassion, built a practice for that moment. It takes one hand and a few plain words, and it's small enough to do in a parked car.

teach.b: First, three parts. Neff describes self-compassion as having three pieces. Mindfulness: noticing that this is a moment of suffering, without blowing it up or brushing it off.
Common humanity: remembering that suffering is part of being human. Not, others have it worse.

teach.h: THIS IS HARD. OTHERS FEEL THIS TOO.
teach.b: Others feel this too. And kindness: treating yourself the way you'd treat a friend who was hurting. Second, the short version.
In what she calls a self-compassion break, those three pieces become three plain moves. Something like: this is hard. Others feel this too.
And a wish to be kind to yourself, in whatever words fit. People choose their own words. The three moves matter more than a script.
Neff suggests a soothing touch, a hand on the heart or wherever feels comforting, as a way of telling the body what the words are telling the mind. Fourth, the week.

It began in the lab and the clinic: soften around it, posttraumatic growth, Elijah. Then it turned to practices for hard days: tonglen, qinah, less advice. Several of those point outward, toward someone else's pain.
Today turns the same care inward.
Less advice and more presence works on the inside, too.

how: Kristin Neff teaches a short self-compassion break: noticing a moment of suffering, remembering that others feel it too, and offering oneself kindness, sometimes with a hand on the heart.

o: a novelist who wrote about a family's grief
a pastor who wrote about suffering and faith

games.q: Neff's three parts — tap the pairs.
p: this is a moment of suffering
on the heart, or wherever is comforting

s: common humanity means your pain doesn't count because others have it worse
it means others feel this too, not that yours matters less.
the practice only works with exact words

games.q: something stings today. the inner voice starts in like a drill sergeant. what's the self-compassion break's first move?
o: notice it plainly: this is hard.
compare it to someone who has it worse.
games.why: first, mindfulness: noticing that this is a moment of suffering. then, others feel this too, and a kind wish for yourself.

practice: Bring to mind something mildly hard from today and, if it feels okay, place a hand on your heart or wherever is comforting. Quietly, in your own words: this is hard; others feel this too; and one kind wish for yourself.
Then let the hand rest or drop, and just breathe; if you pray, you can bring the same three moves to God.

wordCard.voice: Kristin Neff, the psychologist whose self-compassion break pairs noticing, common humanity, and kindness toward yourself. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: others feel this too. The care you'd give a friend has room for you as well. Day seven hundred forty-two.
